openers.key-ecosystems: Forests, wetlands, grasslands and peatlands are not interchangeable patches of green. A forest is an ecosystem defined by a dense community of trees; a grassland is one dominated by grasses; a wetland is ground flooded or soaked with water for all or part of the year. Some of these places hide their importance underground or underwater, like the peat that builds up in a bog from dead moss. Each kind works differently, and each gives people different benefits, such as the water that wetlands store and clean. This chapter tours the main kinds, from tropical rainforest and northern taiga to mangrove coasts, and asks what each one does and what happens when it is lost.

nature-eco-567.title: Forests: where most of Earth's plant life stands
nature-eco-567.text: Forests contain 80% of Earth's plant biomass, the total weight of living plant matter. They also account for 75% of the biosphere's gross primary production, the plant growth powered by sunlight. A forest is an ecosystem defined by a dense community of trees. Pinning that down is harder than it sounds, and there are hundreds of definitions. The FAO, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, offers one. It counts land over 0.5 hectares with trees taller than 5 metres and more than 10 percent canopy cover. Land that is mainly farm or urban does not count. By that measure the world has 4.14 billion hectares of forest: 32% of global land area, or 0.50 ha per person. Some 45% of it lies in the tropics. Forests give oxygen, carbon storage, clean water, flood control, timber, genetic reserves and recreation, regulate climate and rainfall, and support millions who live from them directly. That bounty is shrinking. Global forest area fell by 178 million hectares between 1990 and 2020, about the size of Libya. Most clearing now happens in the tropics, driven mainly by four commodities: wood, beef, soy and palm oil. Loss can flip a forest's role. If its plant diversity, density or area declines, a forest can turn from a carbon sink into a carbon source. Some researchers add a caution: forests can also impose costs, such as taking land from grazing and crops or reducing available water.

nature-eco-498.title: Aquatic ecosystems: life organized around water
nature-eco-498.text: Algae may be the most important producers in water, building living matter from carbon dioxide and sunlight. They anchor the aquatic ecosystem: the community of living things in and around a body of water, as opposed to a land-based terrestrial ecosystem. Its organisms depend on each other and on their surroundings. The two main kinds are salty {{ref:nature-eco-499}} systems and {{ref:nature-eco-502}} systems. Fresh waters split further. Lentic waters are still, like ponds and lakes; lotic waters flow, like rivers; and the third type is the soaked ground covered in {{ref:nature-eco-441}}. Water holds relatively little oxygen, so its residents must adapt. Some waterlogged plants grow aerenchyma, a spongy tissue of air channels that carries oxygen to their roots. Where algae and shallow-water plants grow together, as in estuaries and soaked shallows, productivity becomes extraordinary, feeding fish, birds and amphibians.

nature-eco-441.title: Wetlands: the ground between water and land
nature-eco-441.text: In 2005 the {{ref:nature-es-001}} found wetlands more threatened by environmental degradation than any other ecosystem. A wetland is a semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or soaked with water, either permanently or for part of the year. It sits between open water and dry land, and its plants have roots adapted to oxygen-poor, waterlogged soils. The single most important factor in making one is hydrology: how long and how often an area floods. Wetlands exist on every continent except Antarctica, and their water may be fresh, brackish (slightly salty) or salt. They come in several forms. Marshes are dominated by reeds, cattails and sedges, swamps by trees and shrubs, while bogs and fens build up peat. The largest include the Amazon basin, the West Siberian Plain, the Pantanal and the Sundarbans. Wetlands are among the most biologically diverse ecosystems. Their plants improve water quality by removing excess nitrates and phosphorus, two nutrients that pollute rivers. They also purify water, stabilize shorelines, protect against storms and control floods, which makes their loss costly.

nature-eco-410.title: Mangroves: trees that live in the sea's edge
nature-eco-410.text: Most plants die in salt water. Mangroves thrive in it. A mangrove is a tree or shrub that lives mostly in salty or brackish coastal water. The word also names the coastal vegetation these plants form, a kind of {{ref:nature-eco-441}}. Special adaptations let them take in extra oxygen and get rid of salt. They grow along tropical and subtropical coasts, mostly between 30° N and 30° S, with the largest area within 5° of the equator. In 2025 the world's mangroves were estimated to cover 15.9 million hectares, with Asia holding the largest share at 6.10 million ha. Just five countries, Indonesia, Brazil, Australia, Nigeria and Mexico, hold almost half (49%) of the global area. A stand of mangroves has few tree species, yet it shelters many other species, including up to 174 species of marine megafauna, the large sea animals. Mangroves support coastal and ocean life, shield nearby land from tsunamis and extreme weather, and store carbon well. People keep destroying them anyway, at an estimated 0.16% a year worldwide and up to 0.70% a year in some countries. A 2022 study estimated a net loss of 3,700 km2 of mangroves between 1999 and 2019.

nature-eco-467.title: Grasslands: the open biome that feeds herds
nature-eco-467.text: Grasslands support the greatest gatherings of large animals on Earth. A grassland is an area or ecosystem whose vegetation is dominated by grasses. They occur naturally on every continent except Antarctica and rank among the largest biomes, covering somewhere between 31–69% of Earth's land area depending on how they are counted. Some are natural, some semi-natural, some agricultural. One definition describes grasslands as places kept open by fire, grazing, drought or freezing temperatures, the forces that stop trees from taking over. Their value is easy to miss because much of it lies underground. Grasslands hold about twenty percent of all the carbon stored in the world's soils. Their marketed and non-marketed ecosystem services, those sold for money and those that never reach a market, are fundamental to the livelihoods of an estimated one billion people. Yet grasslands have been described as the most imperiled land biome, converted faster than forests and given little protection.

nature-eco-475.title: Peatlands: wetlands built from half-rotted plants
nature-eco-475.text: Peatlands cover around 3 million km2, yet they are the largest natural carbon store on land. A peatland is a wetland whose soil is made of layers of peat, partly decayed plant material. Peat builds up because waterlogging cuts off oxygen. Without oxygen, the microbes that break down dead plant litter work slowly, so the litter only partly decomposes and accumulates year after year. The result is staggering. Peat soils store over 600 Gt of carbon, more than all other vegetation types, forests included. Peatlands are most extensive at high northern latitudes. Left intact, they reduce flood risk and erosion, purify water and help regulate climate. They face three main threats: peat harvesting, drainage for farming, notably for palm oil in the tropics, and fire. Destroying a peatland reverses its gift. The greenhouse gases it locked away escape into the air, worsening climate change.

nature-eco-442.title: What wetlands do for people, and what they are worth
nature-eco-442.text: One analysis valued the storm protection wetlands provide against hurricanes at US$33,000/hectare/year. That is one of many ecosystem services, the benefits people get from nature, that wetlands supply by storing and cleaning water. The {{ref:nature-es-001}} and the {{ref:nature-gov-051}} list a long roster: flood control, refilling of underground water, storm protection, cleaning of water, biodiversity, products, culture, recreation and a steadier climate. Many wetlands are linked to water stored underground and help refill the porous rock layers that supply much of the world's drinking water. Coastal wetlands protect shores by reducing the speed and height of waves and floodwaters. In highly developed areas, wetlands may be the only habitat left for pollinating insects, birds and mammals. Replacing these services would take enormous sums for treatment plants, dams and levees, and many could not be replaced at all. According to the Ramsar treaty, intact wetlands are often worth much more to society than the gains people expect from converting them to intensive use.

nature-eco-562.title: Tropical forests: half the world's species on a fifth of its land
nature-eco-562.text: Tropical forests cover less than one-fifth of Earth's land yet hold about 50% of the world's species. They also hold about 60 percent of vascular plants, the plants with internal tubes for water. They are the forested regions with tropical climates, roughly between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. The tropical domain holds the largest share of the world's forests, 45 percent, ahead of boreal, temperate and subtropical forests. The label covers more than steamy jungle. It includes evergreen rainforests, open eucalyptus forest, tropical conifer forest, savanna woodland and mountain cloud forests. Because no single scheme defines a forest, estimates of their extent vary between sources. Much current clearing in these biodiversity-rich places is driven by exports of beef, soy, coffee, cacao, palm oil and timber. Putting a value on the forests' ecosystem services is widely held to encourage sustainable policy, but only with clear monitoring of what actually happens.

nature-eco-563.title: Tropical rainforests: rain every month, poor soil below
nature-eco-563.text: Coffee, chocolate, bananas, mangoes and sugarcane all came originally from tropical rainforests. A tropical rainforest is a dense, warm forest with high rainfall, typically within 10° north and south of the Equator. True rainforests have no dry season: every month averages at least 60 mm of rain, and mean monthly temperatures exceed 18 °C. All that rain has a cost. It leaches, or washes out, nutrients, so soils are often poor. Most nutrients sit near the surface, because fallen leaves and dead organisms decompose quickly. Above ground, life is lavish. Rainforests have among the highest primary production of any land ecosystem and produce about 30% of Earth's fresh water. They maintain biodiversity, store carbon, regulate climate and support the animals that carry pollen; forests produce half of the Amazon's own rainfall. Mining, drilling and conversion to farmland drive their clearing, and mineral and fossil-fuel extraction is often prioritised for economic growth. One response is REDD, a market incentive through which companies and governments offset their emissions by paying for rainforest conservation.

nature-eco-550.title: Old-growth forests: centuries in the making
nature-eco-550.text: After a severe disturbance, a regrowing forest can take from a century to several millennia to regain old-growth character. An old-growth forest is one that has developed over a long time without disturbance. It shows its age in big living and dead trees, gappy layered canopies and fallen wood. That varied structure offers more diverse habitat than younger forests and shelters many rare and endangered species. It also stores carbon more productively than younger forests. Its services, from clean air and water to pest control, may matter more than its timber. The FAO's related term is primary forest: naturally regenerated native forest with no clearly visible human activity. One-third (34%) of the world's forests are primary. As of January 2009 only 21% of Earth's original old-growth forests remained, and 90% of those in the contiguous United States in the 1600s have been cleared. Loss is slowing: primary forest disappeared at 1.61 million ha a year in 2015–2025, less than half the 3.92 million ha a year of 2000–2015.

nature-eco-559.title: The taiga: Earth's great northern forest
nature-eco-559.text: The taiga stores more carbon than the world's temperate and tropical forests combined. Also called the boreal forest, it is a biome of mostly pine, spruce and larch across the high northern latitudes. It lies between the treeless {{ref:nature-eco-565}} to the north and the forests of milder latitudes to the south. It covers 17 million km2, or 11.5% of Earth's land, with the largest areas in Russia and Canada. Life here is cold. Mean annual temperatures generally run from −5 to 5 °C, summers last 1–3 months and freezing winters 5–7 months. The cold slows soil development, so soils are young and nutrient-poor. Much of the taiga's carbon sits in wetlands and peat, and per unit area it holds about twice as much as tropical forests. Protecting it can be a bargain: fire management costs about 12 dollars per tonne of carbon kept from release, very cheap compared with the {{ref:nature-clim-241}}. Its latitudes saw some of Earth's largest temperature increases in the last quarter of the twentieth century, and fewer extreme cold days have helped tree-damaging insects.

nature-eco-508.title: Bogs: where decay runs slower than growth
nature-eco-508.text: The world's largest wetland is a bog: the peat bogs of the Western Siberian Lowlands, covering more than a million square kilometres. A bog is a wetland that builds up peat, a deposit of dead plant matter, usually sphagnum moss. It is one of the four main types of wetland. Bogs form where surface water is acidic and poor in nutrients, mostly in cooler northern climates. Most get their water and nutrients from rain rather than from ground or surface water. Plants grow slowly here, but decay is even slower in the oxygen-poor, waterlogged soil, so peat piles up, sometimes many meters deep and usually thicker than 30 centimetres. Specialized species cope with the scarcity, such as carnivorous sundews and pitcher plants that get nutrients from insects. Because plant material keeps accumulating, a bog is a carbon sink. Peat-forming mires that are alkaline rather than acidic are called fens instead.

nature-eco-565.title: Tundra: the land too cold for trees
nature-eco-565.text: Arctic tundra is a desert of sorts, with about 150–250 mm of precipitation a year and winter temperatures around −28 °C. Tundra is a biome where freezing temperatures and short growing seasons keep trees from growing. The boundary between tundra and forest is the tree line. There are three types, Arctic, Alpine and Antarctic, and their vegetation is low: dwarf shrubs, sedges, grasses, mosses and lichens. Biodiversity is limited to about 1,700 vascular plant species and 48 land mammal species, though millions of birds migrate there each summer. The frozen soils store biomass as carbon, making tundra soil a carbon sink. Beneath it lies another kind of wealth. Arctic tundra is rich in petroleum, natural gas and uranium, and Russia's Yamalo-Nenets region produces 90% of the country's natural gas.

nature-eco-568.title: The forest transition: when losing turns to gaining
nature-eco-568.text: Net forest loss worldwide fell from 7.8 million hectares a year in the 1990s to 4.7 million hectares a year in 2010–2020. New forests offset part of the clearing. Behind that shift lies the forest transition: the change of a region from losing forest to gaining forested land overall. Countries tend to move through stages. They start with high forest cover and low clearing, pass through fast clearing and low cover, then see loss slow, stabilize and reverse. The gain comes three ways: commercial plantations of trees, small farmers mixing trees with crops, or natural regrowth on abandoned farmland. The drivers vary too. Forests may be valued for timber, for their ecosystem services, or simply for their own sake as culture changes. Large planting programmes in China, India, the United States and Vietnam contributed, and China banned logging from 1998 because of erosion and flooding. In 2025 about 813 million ha, around 20% of forest area, lay on legally protected land. Two cautions apply. New forests are not equal to old-growth forests in species diversity, resilience or carbon capture. And the transition is not a law of nature: population density, stage of development, global markets and policy all shape it.

nature-eco-447.title: Wetland loss: two-thirds gone since 1900
nature-eco-447.text: Since 1900, 65–70% of the world's wetlands have been lost. Wetlands are damaged or destroyed by drainage, pollution, dams, taking too many fish and other human activities, as well as by natural disturbances. Drainage is the classic story. People cut dykes and ditches to create farmland and raise economic output, and some of the world's key farming areas were once wetlands. The bill can arrive later: settlements built on drained wetlands become prone to sinking ground and rising flood risk. Because wetland water barely flows, toxic pollutants concentrate quickly and harm native species. Shrimp farming has wiped out large areas of mangrove, damage that is hard to curb because global demand is strong. In East Asia, up to 65% of coastal wetlands have been destroyed by coastal development. Damage comes in degrees. Minor and moderate disturbances let a wetland recover on its own; severe ones need human help.

nature-eco-448.title: Wetland conservation: from wasteland to treasure
nature-eco-448.text: More than three billion people, around half the world's population, get their basic water needs from inland freshwater wetlands. Wetland conservation aims to protect these places and their natural functions from draining, flooding and other damaging change. Since the 1970s, more attention has gone to preserving wetlands for what they do. The {{ref:nature-gov-051}}, a treaty at work since 1971, lists wetlands of international importance and promotes their wise use. Its methods include restricting access and teaching the public that wetlands are not wastelands. Wetlands cover at least six percent of Earth and became a conservation focus because of their services. Coastal wetlands are estimated to save a median of US$447 billion in damages and 4,620 lives each year from storms. Wetlands also hold around 700 billion tons of carbon, mainly in peat soils, and take up about 96 million tons more a year. Protection need not cost local people their living. Studies show wetlands can be conserved while improving local livelihoods, as with sustainably farmed dambos, seasonally wet valley grasslands, in Malawi and Zambia.

nature-eco-449.title: Wetland restoration: from letting go to rebuilding
nature-eco-449.text: The cheapest way to restore a damaged wetland is often to stop harming it and step back. Wetland restoration helps a damaged wetland return to its natural path of development by assisting its natural processes. How much help it needs depends on how badly it is disturbed, though budget, time, goals and politics also shape the choice. At the light end, the wetland recovers by natural succession, the gradual return of plant and animal communities, once disturbance stops. In the middle sits partial reconstruction, which mixes natural regrowth with engineering such as ripping compacted subsoil, mulching and mechanical seeding. At the heavy end, complete reconstruction rebuilds the wetland from the ground up, the most expensive and intrusive option. Another resource is {{ref:nature-gov-176}}, the understanding built up by local peoples over generations, offers a holistic approach that can raise wetland productivity, biodiversity and resilience.

nature-eco-451.title: Valuing wetlands: mapping, scoring and ranking
nature-eco-451.text: Agencies often have to judge a wetland after a single visit of less than a day. Valuing wetlands means mapping them, assessing the functions and services each provides, and using that information to rank or prioritize them. Rapid assessment methods score a wetland's functions, services, species and health quickly. They are needed mainly when agencies face decision deadlines or have many wetlands to assess. The results help decide which wetlands to protect and how much compensation a loss requires, such as restoring wetlands elsewhere. Over the longer term, valuation needs wetland inventories and monitoring of a sample to track change. Satellite and aerial imagery, increasingly combined with laser scanning from the air, called {{ref:nature-es-068}}, map and monitor wetlands over large areas.

nature-eco-450.title: Wetlands and climate: carbon store or methane source
nature-eco-450.text: Wetlands are the world's largest natural source of methane, emitting about 20–30% of atmospheric methane, on average 161 Tg a year. A teragram (Tg) is a million tonnes. Wetlands can either store carbon and slow climate change or release greenhouse gases such as methane, depending on the wetland and how it is treated. The reason is in the mud. Waterlogged, oxygen-poor soils favour methane-producing microbes. Drained peat flips the other way and decomposes into carbon dioxide. Peatlands cover only 3% of land, but their degradation produces 7% of all CO2 emissions. Coastal wetlands are strong absorbers. {{ref:nature-eco-428}} and mangroves take up on average 210 g CO2 m−2 y−1, compared with about 20–30 g CO2 m−2 y−1 for peatlands. Even so, restoring coastal wetlands purely to remove CO2, the idea behind {{ref:nature-nbs-034}}, has questionable cost-effectiveness. Their bigger payoff may be adaptation: flood control, underground water supplies and storm protection help societies cope with the worse floods and droughts of a warming climate.

nature-eco-520.title: Drylands: where water is the limit
nature-eco-520.text: Drylands cover 41.3% of Earth's land surface, including 66% of Africa, 40% of Asia, 24% of Europe and 15% of Latin America. They are lands defined by scarce water, where rainfall is balanced by evaporation and the water plants give off. The UN Environment Programme defines them as tropical and temperate areas with an aridity index below 0.65. The aridity index compares rainfall with the water the air could draw off; the lower it is, the drier the land. More than 2 billion people live in drylands, and 72% of drylands lie in developing countries. They include 45% of the world's agricultural land. Their behaviour depends on many linked interactions among climate, soil and vegetation. Unlike humid biomes, drylands move water around mainly through surface runoff. They are highly vulnerable to climate change through shifting rainfall and land degradation.

nature-eco-452.title: Agroecosystems: nature reshaped to grow food
nature-eco-452.text: Forest gardens are probably the world's oldest and most resilient agroecosystem. An agroecosystem is a natural ecosystem that people have modified and manage to produce crops or livestock. Like any ecosystem, it combines a physical environment, living things such as crops and wildlife, and the interactions linking them. It is the basic unit of study in {{ref:nature-nbs-246}} and {{ref:nature-nbs-258}}. Its reach goes beyond the farm gate, to the whole region its activity affects through changes to species, energy flows and nutrient balance. Intensively managed farms simplify those flows, and their excess nutrients cause eutrophication, an overgrowth of algae, downstream. More plant diversity brings both ecological and economic benefits. Some approaches try to blur the line with natural ecosystems, for example through polyculture, growing several crops together, wildlife buffer strips and {{ref:nature-nbs-292}}. A report by the International Water Management Institute and UNEP suggested assigning value to ecosystems and recognizing trade-offs among their users.

nature-es-082.title: Mangroves as a living sea wall
nature-es-082.text: Wave energy may fall by 75 per cent as a wave passes through 200 meters of mangroves. Mangrove swamps act as a natural barrier that protects coasts from erosion, tsunamis and the storm-driven rise in sea level called {{ref:nature-es-119}}. Their huge root systems absorb wave energy. They also slow incoming tides, so sediment settles out, and the mangroves build up the very land they grow on. When waves are strong, shorelines covered by mangroves erode less, or much more slowly, than bare ones. Studies show mangroves give coastal communities measurable economic protection against tropical storms. Keeping mangroves healthy is cheaper than building concrete walls along the shore, which can increase erosion in front of the wall and on neighbouring land. This protection is why mangroves are often targeted by conservation programmes, including national plans to protect wildlife ({{ref:nature-gov-043}}). Clearing them carries a hidden risk too. The sediments beneath trap heavy metals, and removing the trees can release that contamination into seawater.

nature-eco-416.title: Forest ecology: studying the woods as a whole
nature-eco-416.text: Forests cover almost a third of all land, so what happens in them affects the whole biosphere and the human activities it supports. Forest ecology is the scientific study of the living things, patterns and processes found in forest ecosystems. A forest ecosystem is all the plants, animals and microbes of a woodland working together with their non-living surroundings. Forest ecologists usually study whole populations, communities or ecosystems rather than single organisms. Trees vary hugely in size and arrangement, so forests are patchy, varied environments, and that variety supports great biodiversity. Managing forests goes by several names, including {{ref:nature-res-131}} and {{ref:nature-res-156}}. Machine learning now lets forest ecologists process larger and more complex data sets.
